items: base64url parts joined by dots — self-contained, no lookup
Header names the algorithm; payload holds the claims
Standard claims: `iss` `sub` `aud` `exp` `nbf` `iat` `jti`
`exp` and `aud` are the two people forget to verify

blocks.title: Encoding, Not Encryption
blocks.text: Anyone can paste a JWT into a decoder and read the payload. Never put a password, PII, or any secret inside one.

items: With HS256, every verifier can also mint tokens
`alg: none` attack comes from trusting the header
So does HS256/RS256 confusion
Pin the expected algorithm server-side, always
Stateless verification is fast and scales flat
You cannot revoke a token before `exp`
Workarounds: 5–15 min access tokens
Or a `jti` denylist, or a token-version column
Each workaround reintroduces the state you removed
Short access token in memory or a cookie
Long-lived refresh token in an `HttpOnly` cookie
Scope it narrow: `Path=/auth/refresh`
Rotate: each refresh issues a new one, kills the old
A reused old token means theft — kill the whole family

left.title: localStorage
items: popular bad advice
any XSS reads it
no `HttpOnly` available

right.title: Secure cookie
items: XSS protection back
takes on CSRF
CSRF is easier to defend

blocks.title: Bearer Headers Dodge CSRF
blocks.text: `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` is immune by construction — the browser never attaches it automatically. Genuinely right for cross-service auth, mobile and native clients, third-party APIs, short-lived grants.

blocks.title: Clock Skew
items: Allow 30–60s leeway on `exp` and `nbf`
Otherwise distributed servers reject valid tokens
Symptom: intermittent 401s on one node only

left.title: Session
items: server-side store
opaque random ID
instant delete

right.title: Token
items: self-contained
signed claims
valid until `exp`

blocks.title: Size Is Per Request
blocks.text: A 700-byte JWT rides on every single call, including static assets on the same host. The session cookie stays under 64 bytes forever.

items: Sessions are simply easier to get right
Tokens need refresh, rotation and key management
Complexity is a real cost, not a style preference
Server-rendered app or first-party SPA on one domain
Then sessions in `__Host-` cookies, done
Use tokens for multiple backend services
Or a public API, native mobile apps, third-party integrations

blocks.title: The Common Hybrid
blocks.text: Session cookie for the browser UI, plus a short-lived JWT minted per request for service-to-service calls. Best of both, one auth surface.

items: Flow: verify credentials, create record, return the ID
The cookie carries only an opaque random ID
User, roles and expiry all live server-side
Each request: look up the store, attach the user
Logout deletes the record — the ID dies everywhere

blocks.title: Store Pitfalls
items: In-memory stores break horizontal scaling
Symptom: random logouts after every deploy
Set TTL at the store level (Redis `EXPIRE`)
Else dead sessions accumulate forever

blocks.title: Signed Cookie Sessions
blocks.text: Rails and Flask style puts the data IN the cookie with an HMAC — no store to run, but no revocation either, and the 4KB cap bites fast.

items: Rate-limit the login endpoint
Hash with argon2 or bcrypt, never SHA-family
Ship MFA
These matter more than the transport choice
Missing `Secure`/`HttpOnly` because dev config got copied
Assert flags in a startup check, not a code review
Default `Path` swallowing the cookie set at `/api/login`
It never reaches `/dashboard` — always `Path=/`
Delete fails when `Domain`/`Path` differ from the original
Cookie survives, user stays logged in
Two same-name cookies: one host-only, one `Domain=`
Server reads the wrong one — inspect the raw `Cookie` header
Not the parsed map, which silently keeps one

blocks.title: Dropped Without A Word
blocks.text: `SameSite=None` without `Secure` and the browser discards the cookie entirely — you get a console warning and nothing else.

items: OAuth callbacks and payment redirects die under `Strict`
The return leg is a cross-site POST
No regeneration on login = session fixation
Attacker plants an ID, victim logs in, attacker owns it
JWT in `localStorage` 'for convenience' — one XSS empties it

blocks.text: Lax Is Not A GET Excuse

items: Lax still rides on cross-site top-level GETs
So `/delete?id=5` stays CSRF-able under Lax
Never mutate state on a GET route
Two-cookie pattern: Lax to read, Strict to write
Chrome's 2-minute Lax+POST grace — never rely on it
Cookies are fully attacker-controlled input
Sign them, validate them, never SQL-interpolate them
4KB overflow truncates or drops silently
Happens when roles or flash messages bloat a signed session

lines: // name + Domain + Path must all match

blocks.title: Debug Toolkit
items: DevTools, Application, Cookies — shows every flag
`curl -v` for what the wire really carries
`document.cookie` hides `HttpOnly` — that is the point
Network tab's Cookies pane logs rejections with a reason

blocks.title: Check Chrome First
blocks.text: Chrome states exactly why it dropped a cookie in the Network tab. Read that before blaming your server code.

items: `__Host-` prefix, `Secure`, `HttpOnly`
`SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`
Absolute plus idle timeout, both
Regenerate on login, delete server-side on logout

blocks.title: One Line
blocks.text: Cookies are automatic, scoped by site not origin, and attacker-visible — so sign them, flag them, scope them tight, and keep the real state on the server.

caption.text: Part 2 of HTTP COOKIES & WEB AUTH. Your session cookie is one missing attribute away from being someone else's. This field manual walks every `Set-Cookie` attribute, why `Path` silently eats your login, how a compromised subdomain can overwrite a cookie it should never touch, and where SameSite actually stops CSRF versus where it just looks like it does. Ends with the session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist you can paste into your auth PR.
